quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The woman _____ lives next door is a doctor.
quests.sentence: The woman _____ lives next door is a doctor.
quests.hint: 'Who' refers to people as the subject of the relative clause.
quests.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person as the subject. 'Which' is for things. 'Whom' is the object form of 'who' - not the subject.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The phone _____ I bought last week is already broken.
quests.sentence: The phone _____ I bought last week is already broken.
quests.hint: 'That' (or 'which') introduces a defining relative clause about a thing; don't add 'is'.
quests.explanation: In a defining relative clause about a thing, 'that' or 'which' is used. Adding 'is' after 'which' would create a second finite verb, breaking the clause structure.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The restaurant _____ we visited last week has closed.
quests.sentence: The restaurant _____ we visited last week has closed.
quests.hint: The object relative clause about a place: use 'that' or 'which', not 'where' or 'it'.
quests.explanation: 'That' (or 'which') is the object pronoun in this defining relative clause. 'Where' can only introduce relative clauses when it replaces a prepositional phrase of place ('the restaurant where we ate'), not the object position here.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The manager _____ hired me has retired.
quests.sentence: The manager _____ hired me has retired.
quests.hint: 'Who' is the subject of 'hired me' in this relative clause.
quests.explanation: 'Who' is the subject form - it is the manager who performed the action ('hired me'). 'Whom' is the object form, used when the relative pronoun is the object of the verb.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The student _____ essay won first prize is from India.
quests.sentence: The student _____ essay won first prize is from India.
quests.hint: 'Whose' shows possession - the student's essay won.
quests.explanation: 'Whose' is the possessive relative pronoun, replacing 'his/her'. 'The student whose essay won' = 'the student; his/her essay won'. Neither 'who' nor 'whom' can show possession.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The person _____ I spoke to was very helpful.
quests.sentence: The person _____ I spoke to was very helpful.
quests.hint: 'Whom' is the object of 'spoke to' - use the object form here.
quests.explanation: 'Whom' is the object form of 'who'. In the relative clause, 'I spoke to [them]' - the pronoun is the object of the preposition 'to'. Formal English uses 'whom' for this object position.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: My brother, _____ is a chef, works in a five-star hotel.
quests.sentence: My brother, _____ is a chef, works in a five-star hotel.
quests.hint: Non-defining relative clauses about people use 'who', never 'that'.
quests.explanation: In non-defining relative clauses (set off by commas), 'that' is never used - only 'who' for people or 'which' for things. The commas show the information is additional, not essential.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The Eiffel Tower, _____ is in Paris, attracts millions of visitors each year.
quests.sentence: The Eiffel Tower, _____ is in Paris, attracts millions of visitors each year.
quests.hint: Non-defining relative clause about a thing → 'which' (no commas with 'that').
quests.explanation: 'Which' introduces non-defining relative clauses about things. 'That' is never used with non-defining clauses (the ones between commas). 'Who' is for people; 'where' introduces place relative clauses, not noun-modifying clauses like this.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: She gave me a gift, _____ surprised me greatly.
quests.sentence: She gave me a gift, _____ surprised me greatly.
quests.hint: 'Which' can refer to the whole previous clause or idea - 'that' cannot do this.
quests.explanation: 'Which' can refer to the whole idea of the previous clause ('she gave me a gift'). 'That' cannot do this, and 'what' is not a relative pronoun here. This is a non-defining relative clause commenting on the entire preceding action.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The company _____ I work for is very successful.
quests.sentence: The company _____ I work for is very successful.
quests.hint: Informal English: keep the preposition at the end and use 'that' or no pronoun.
quests.explanation: In informal English, prepositions stay at the end of the relative clause: '... that I work for'. In formal English, the preposition moves to the front: '... for which I work'. Both are correct, but 'which for' is never acceptable word order.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The hotel _____ we stayed was excellent.
quests.sentence: The hotel _____ we stayed was excellent.
quests.hint: 'Where' replaces 'which we stayed in/at' when referring to a location in a defining clause.
quests.explanation: 'Where' elegantly replaces 'which ... in/at' for locations. 'The hotel where we stayed' = 'the hotel in which we stayed'. 'Which we stayed' (without a preposition) leaves the clause grammatically incomplete.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: 2010 was the year _____ they got married.
quests.sentence: 2010 was the year _____ they got married.
quests.hint: 'When' introduces time relative clauses, replacing 'in which' for years/times.
quests.explanation: 'When' = 'in which' for time expressions. 'The year when they got married' is more natural than 'the year in which they got married', though both are correct. 'That' is possible here too, but 'which' alone is not.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: She enjoys _____ to music while she works.
quests.sentence: She enjoys _____ to music while she works.
quests.hint: 'Enjoy' is always followed by a gerund (-ing form), never an infinitive.
quests.explanation: 'Enjoy' is one of the verbs that must be followed by a gerund. 'Enjoy to listen' is incorrect in standard English. Other gerund-only verbs include 'avoid', 'suggest', 'finish', 'mind', and 'stop' (when it means 'cease').

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: They suggested _____ a different route.
quests.sentence: They suggested _____ a different route.
quests.hint: 'Suggest' is always followed by a gerund, not an infinitive.
quests.explanation: 'Suggest + gerund' is the correct pattern. 'Suggest to take' is a common learner error. Other gerund-following verbs: 'recommend', 'avoid', 'consider', 'deny'.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: He stopped _____ cigarettes three years ago.
quests.sentence: He stopped _____ cigarettes three years ago.
quests.hint: 'Stop + gerund' means 'cease doing' - 'stop to smoke' means something very different (stop in order to smoke).
quests.explanation: 'Stop + gerund' means to cease an activity: 'stopped smoking' = quit. 'Stop + infinitive' means to stop in order to do something else: 'stopped to smoke' = paused and smoked. These have entirely different meanings.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: She decided _____ a new career.
quests.sentence: She decided _____ a new career.
quests.hint: 'Decide' is always followed by an infinitive (to + base verb).
quests.explanation: 'Decide' takes an infinitive: 'decided to pursue'. It cannot take a gerund. Other infinitive-only verbs: 'want', 'plan', 'hope', 'refuse', 'choose', 'expect', 'agree'.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: They plan _____ a new business next year.
quests.sentence: They plan _____ a new business next year.
quests.hint: 'Plan' is followed by an infinitive, not a gerund.
quests.explanation: 'Plan to + base verb' is always correct. 'Plan on + gerund' is an informal but accepted alternative, but 'plan starting' without a preposition is ungrammatical.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: He hopes _____ a scholarship.
quests.sentence: He hopes _____ a scholarship.
quests.hint: 'Hope' takes an infinitive: 'hope to do something'.
quests.explanation: 'Hope' is always followed by an infinitive. 'Hope to receive' = want to receive (with positive expectation). 'Hoping' after 'hope' would require 'is hoping for', a different structure entirely.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: I remember _____ her at the conference. (She was there; I saw her.)
quests.sentence: I remember _____ her at the conference. (She was there; I saw her.)
quests.hint: 'Remember + gerund' = recall a past event. 'Remember + infinitive' = don't forget to do something future.
quests.explanation: 'Remember + gerund' recalls something from the past: 'I remember meeting her' = I have a memory of meeting her. 'Remember + infinitive' refers to a duty: 'Remember to meet her' = don't forget your appointment with her.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: Don't forget _____ the lights when you leave.
quests.sentence: Don't forget _____ the lights when you leave.
quests.hint: 'Forget + infinitive' = fail to do something upcoming. 'Forget + gerund' = fail to recall a past event.
quests.explanation: 'Forget + infinitive' refers to future responsibilities: 'Don't forget to turn off the lights' = remember to do it. 'Forget + gerund' refers to memory of past events: 'I'll never forget meeting her'.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: She tried _____ the machine, but it still didn't work.
quests.sentence: She tried _____ the machine, but it still didn't work.
quests.hint: 'Try + gerund' = experiment with a method. 'Try + infinitive' = make an effort to do something difficult.
quests.explanation: 'Try + gerund' means to experiment with an approach ('tried restarting' = tried that approach to solve it). 'Try + infinitive' means to attempt something difficult ('tried to restart' = made the effort). Both are possible here, but the context implies experimenting with a method.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: _____ regularly is important for your health.
quests.sentence: _____ regularly is important for your health.
quests.hint: When an -ing form acts as the subject of a sentence, it is a gerund.
quests.explanation: A gerund (verb + -ing) can function as the subject of a sentence. 'Exercising regularly is important' treats the activity as a noun. The infinitive 'to exercise' could also work as a subject, but it sounds more formal and less natural here.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: She's good at _____ problems quickly.
quests.sentence: She's good at _____ problems quickly.
quests.hint: After a preposition ('at'), always use a gerund, never an infinitive.
quests.explanation: Prepositions must be followed by a noun or gerund, never a bare infinitive or 'to + verb'. 'Good at solving' is correct because 'at' is a preposition requiring a gerund.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: Instead of _____ a cab, why not walk?
quests.sentence: Instead of _____ a cab, why not walk?
quests.hint: After the preposition 'of', use the gerund form.
quests.explanation: 'Instead of' is a prepositional phrase and must be followed by a gerund. 'Instead of taking' is correct. 'Instead of to take' is wrong because infinitives never follow prepositions.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The teacher made the students _____ the test again.
quests.sentence: The teacher made the students _____ the test again.
quests.hint: 'Make' in this causative sense takes a bare infinitive (no 'to').
quests.explanation: 'Make + object + bare infinitive' expresses compulsion. 'Made them repeat' - no 'to'. If you change 'make' to 'allow' or 'permit', you need 'to': 'allowed them to repeat'.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: She let her children _____ up late on weekends.
quests.sentence: She let her children _____ up late on weekends.
quests.hint: 'Let' is followed by a bare infinitive - no 'to'.
quests.explanation: 'Let + object + bare infinitive' means to allow. No 'to' is used after 'let'. 'Allowed them to stay' would be the 'to + infinitive' equivalent using 'allow' instead.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: I heard someone _____ outside my window last night.
quests.sentence: I heard someone _____ outside my window last night.
quests.hint: Perception verbs ('hear/see/watch') take either bare infinitive or -ing; -ing stresses ongoing action.
quests.explanation: After perception verbs ('hear', 'see', 'watch'), both bare infinitive and -ing are possible. 'Heard someone knock' (completed action) and 'heard someone knocking' (ongoing action) are both correct. Here, knocking implies the sound was ongoing - more natural than 'knock'.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The doctor _____ treated my mother has won several awards.
quests.sentence: The doctor _____ treated my mother has won several awards.
quests.hint: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about the doctor (a person, subject position).
quests.explanation: 'Who' is correct as the subject of 'treated'. 'Whom' would be the object. 'Which' is for things. 'That' could replace 'who' in defining clauses but 'that she' adds a redundant subject.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: She admitted _____ the report without reading it.
quests.sentence: She admitted _____ the report without reading it.
quests.hint: 'Admit' is always followed by a gerund, never an infinitive.
quests.explanation: 'Admit + gerund' is the correct structure. Other 'confessional' verbs that take gerunds: 'deny', 'confess to', 'regret' (past action). 'Admit to signing' is also correct; 'admit signing' is the more common form.

quests.instruction: Turn the statement into a question.
quests.question: The course, _____ starts in September, is fully online.
quests.sentence: The course, _____ starts in September, is fully online.
quests.hint: Non-defining relative clause about a thing → 'which', not 'that'.
quests.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses (inside commas) use 'which' for things, never 'that'. 'It' creates a run-on sentence. 'Who' is only for people.
